source.label: Fenollosa: Eitoku conceived “great panels … where coarsely drawn but dignified figures of Chinese worthies should crowd a ground”
Fenollosa: court scenes of “Chinese lords and ladies, Emperors and their suites”

work.text: And when Hideyoshi, after his triumph of 1582, began to carve out a Court career, Yeitoku was on hand to conceive great panels of, say, forty feet in length by fifteen in height, where coarsely drawn but dignified figures of Chinese worthies should crowd a ground already largely prepared with gold.

source.author: Ernest F. Fenollosa
source.title: Epochs of Chinese and Japanese Art, Vol. II

work.text: while his importance is fairly clear there are few if any certain attributions to him, especially to his hand alone; in the larger works attributed to him he probably worked together with one of more other artists of the school.

moment.text: The art that should decorate their enormous and brilliant walls should consist of great Tang Court pageants crowded with figures of Chinese lords and ladies, Emperors and their suites, in the most gorgeous costume, and backed by endless reaches of pavilions in enamelled architecture, and of gardens stocked with rare plants and animals.

source.author: Ernest F. Fenollosa
source.title: Epochs of Chinese and Japanese Art, Vol. II

matters.text: The animals and plants shown often had moral or perhaps political significance that is not always obvious today
A Japanese warlord's hall hung with the ladies of an ancient Chinese court was a claim to culture as much as to power: China was the classical past every educated Japanese looked back to.
